title: The Spark: Triggers and Event Dispatch

elements.text: One event, one row, status: queued. The control plane takes it from here.

beats.say: You type git push origin main and hit enter. Three seconds later, a green checkmark appears on your pull request.
But between your keystroke and that green tick, GitHub did not just 'run your code.' It reacted to an event. Let's follow that event.
Four triggers can start a workflow: a git push, a pull request, a cron schedule, or a manual button press in the UI.
All four funnel into the same mechanism: a POST to GitHub's API webhook endpoint.
The payload carries event_type, ref, repository, and a timestamp. That JSON packet is the spark that everything downstream reacts to.
The API reads the payload's event_type and ref, then scans every file in .github/workflows/ looking for one whose triggers match.
The matching YAML is parsed into a tree: each job gets its own list of steps, a runner label like ubuntu-latest, and its own environment.
On the server side, a new row is appended to the workflow-runs ledger. Run number four-eight-two, status: queued.
That single row is the handoff. The trigger is done; the payload is consumed. From this moment the event belongs to the orchestrator, not to your keystroke.
